title: You Think Hearing No Ruins a Deal, Yet Getting Rejected First Triples Your Chance of Yes
description:
Myth vs. Neural Mechanism — Robert Cialdini (1975): 'Door-in-the-Face' — How Getting Told 'NO!' First Tripled Yeses From 17% to 50%!, grounded in Robert B. Cialdini, Joyce E. Vincent, Stephen K. Lewis, Jose Catalan et al. (1975) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that suppose you need volunteers to chaperone a group of juvenile-detention teenagers on a 2-hour Saturday trip to the city zoo. Walk straight up to strangers on an Arizona State campus walkway (Small Request Only Control, Cialdini et al., 1975 JPSP) and ask politely: 83.3% turn you down flat — only 16.7% say YES.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: Now try Cialdini's 'Door-in-the-Face' (Rejection-Then-Retraction) sequence on the exact same walkway: FIRST, make an outrageous request almost guaranteed to get a door slammed in your face — 'Will you serve as an unpaid counselor for 2 hours every week for the next TWO FULL YEARS?' Predictably, 100% of walkers (24 out of 24) said NO.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Robert B. Cialdini, Joyce E. Vincent, Stephen K. Lewis, Jose Catalan et al. (1975). Reciprocal concessions procedure for inducing compliance: The door-in-the-face technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076284
- Robert B. Cialdini, Karen Ascani (1976). Test of a concession procedure for inducing verbal, behavioral, and further compliance with a request to give blood. Journal of Applied Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.61.3.295
- Thomas Hugh Feeley (2025). 50-Year review of the Door-in-the-Face message strategy. Communication Monographs. https://doi.org/10.1080/03637751.2025.2594987
